rv.q: It's a whip-smart, edge-of-your-seat ride that'd rival anything at Six Flags.
Ultimately, the piece’s strength lies not in its storytelling but in its twisted pageantry.
Even if Enron isn't the last word on the free market debacle, it is a fantastic theatrical event.
The British import 'Enron' is a theatrical roller coaster that captures the dizzying rise and fall of the energy company with inventive staging and compelling performances.

The Expressionistic storytelling techniques devised by Prebble and artfully conceptualized by helmer Goold clarify the complexity of all the crooked high finance while holding it up to raucous ridicule.
But for all its undeniable inventiveness, the play is curiously uninvolving.
Prebble's dialogue veers toward hyperbolic, big statements that eventually prove wearying, especially in the overlong and increasingly moralistic second act.
Sleazy, greedy, foolish and tacky they might have been, but those venal bastards were storytellers, showmen par excellence.

Despite the serious research and the playful imagination, the splendid new American cast and the irresistible craven puppets, the play tells us what it is in the first half-hour and then tells us again for another two hours.

Yet even with a well-drilled cast that includes bright Broadway headliners like Norbert Leo Butz and Marin Mazzie, the realization sets in early that this British-born exploration of smoke-and-mirror financial practices isn’t much more than smoke and mirrors itself.
The problem with 'Enron' is that it tries to be too many things at once and winds up being none of them particularly well.
That Prebble and her collaborators can fold the pain and shame of this into a fresh, exhilarating experience is one of the season's more pleasant surprises.
Without manipulation or fraud, "Enron" the play earns a very "Strong Buy."
Prebble's writing and the production dreamed up by director Rupert Goold are stunning enough to provide steady wonder, involvement and delight.
Jeffrey Keith Skilling, the former president of Enron Corp., has been quietly serving a 24-year sentence at a federal prison in Colorado.
Too often, in fact, Enron plays like 60 Minutes on acid.
Her play is like a big, shiny, beautifully wrapped package that once eagerly ripped opened reveals a horde of Styrofoam peanuts through which you search vainly for the anticipated present.
The play has a harder time becoming a taut work of modern theater.
For the most part, Prebble cuts a clear narrative through this unwieldy terrain.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this flashy British import about corporate greed. While some praise its theatrical inventiveness and entertaining energy, others find it labored and unfocused, with excessive exposition undermining its ambitious satire.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.
